name: Gas and Fees
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Nothing on a Blockchain Runs for Free
lesson.summary: Gas is the unit that measures how much computational work a transaction or smart contract call requires, and the resulting fee is what users pay to compensate the network for performing and recording that work.
lesson.body:
Every operation a blockchain performs, whether it is a simple transfer of value or a complex smart contract call, consumes real computational resources across every node that must process and verify it. Gas is the accounting unit that measures this consumption. Each individual operation, such as writing a value to storage, performing arithmetic, or checking a signature, has a defined gas cost reflecting roughly how expensive that operation is to execute and verify across the network. A transaction's total gas usage is simply the sum of the costs of everything it does.

The connection to transactions and smart contracts is direct and necessary. A plain transaction that moves value from one address to another consumes a fixed, relatively small amount of gas, commonly cited as 21,000 units on Ethereum for a basic transfer. A transaction that calls into a smart contract, however, might trigger dozens of internal operations, storage updates, and even calls to other contracts, and its gas usage scales with all of that activity, sometimes reaching hundreds of thousands of units for something like a multi-step token swap on a decentralized exchange. Gas is what makes it possible to charge proportionally for the actual computational burden a piece of code creates, rather than charging every transaction the same flat amount regardless of complexity.

Gas also solves a security problem that pure computation cannot solve on its own. Without some cost attached to execution, nothing would stop a contract from containing an infinite loop that could stall block production for the entire network. Because each transaction specifies a maximum amount of gas its sender is willing to pay for, once execution consumes that limit without finishing, it halts automatically, the transaction fails, and the sender loses only the gas already spent rather than the network hanging indefinitely.

The price attached to each unit of gas is set by an ongoing market rather than a fixed protocol constant. Block space is limited, so when many users want their transactions processed quickly, they compete by offering to pay more per unit of gas, and validators or miners naturally prioritize the transactions offering the highest payment. This produces the fee spikes that users of popular blockchain networks are familiar with during periods of high demand, and it is why the same transaction can cost dramatically different amounts depending purely on network congestion at the moment it is sent.

Ethereum's 2021 upgrade known as EIP-1559 changed some of the specific mechanics without changing the underlying concept: it introduced a base fee, automatically adjusted up or down block by block based on how full recent blocks have been, which gets burned rather than paid to the block producer, alongside an optional tip that users add to prioritize inclusion. The core idea gas measures the cost of computation, and fees compensate the network for performing it, remains exactly the same regardless of which specific fee mechanism a given blockchain uses.
